notes.body:
Picture a lamp lit in a dark room: its metal casing is what we do, the wiring behind it is what we hold true, and the light itself is worship offered as though we could see Allah. Those three are exactly the components of the spiritual life, and the hadith of Gabriel names them in a deliberate order.

- Submission (اسلام) — the outward acts: the testimony, prayer, fasting, and the giving of زکوۃ.
- Faith (ایمان) — the inner belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day.
- Excellence (احسان) — to worship Allah as though we see Him.

The pairing follows a careful distinction: morals are rules about right and wrong, the outward conduct of a life, while ethics is the deeper conception of the good, the inward باطن from which those rules are born. **Submission is the realm of action** — the body of the شریعۃ, made of prayer, fasting, and giving — so it belongs with morality, the outer. Faith is the framework of conviction that decides why those acts matter at all, so it belongs with ethics, the inner. To swap them would be to mistake a lamp's casing for its design.

Excellence is not the two simply added together. Its own root carries the sense of beauty, so to practise احسان is to make the soul beautiful, and it is the vision of Allah's beauty that awakens every virtue. **That vision is the animating spirit of both belief and deed** — the light itself, not a third object set beside the casing and the wiring.

This is why the Prophet placed it last and defined it as a way of seeing:

أَنْ تَعْبُدَ اللهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَاهُ، فَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ تَرَاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَرَاكَ
'It is to worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you see Him not, yet truly He sees you.'

Remove that awareness and the acts still stand and the beliefs still hold, but as a body without a soul; keep it, and both come alive as one.

notes.quote: which supplies the outer aspects of morality
etymology: اسلام (submission): from the root س-ل-م, which carries the ideas of peace, safety, and wholeness, as in سلام. To submit is to hand oneself over so completely that one is made whole and at peace, and this is why it names the outward surrender of the limbs in action.

ایمان (faith): from the root ء-م-ن, meaning to be safe and secure, and so to trust, as in أمان, safety. Faith is not a leap in the dark but an inner resting in what is trustworthy — to believe is to place one's security in Allah, which is why it names the framework of conviction within.

احسان (excellence): from the root ح-س-ن, whose first meaning is beauty, حُسن. To do احسان is literally to do what is beautiful, so the word ties goodness to beauty of soul — virtue is the soul made lovely, and its opposite, قُبح, is ugliness.

باطن (the inner): from the root ب-ط-ن, connected to بَطن, the belly or interior. It names what lies hidden beneath the surface — here the inward dimension of the good that ethics concerns itself with, as opposed to the outward ظاہر.

notes.body:
The tightened version:

The reading turns on how the words are tied together, not on doctrine. Take the phrase as it stands:

مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ
"from the evil of what He created."
Al-Falaq 113:2

Here شَرّ, evil, is joined to what comes after it in a construct that Arabic calls اضافة — the "X of Y" bond, the way we say "the heat of a fire." That bond makes evil **the property of the created thing, not a thing created in its own right**. The heat belongs to the fire; it is not the fire.

Watch the small word doing the joining. It is مَا, "that which," the object of the verb خَلَقَ, He created. So what Allah brings into being is the thing itself — "what He created" — and evil only clings to it afterward as something that can come out of it. Evil is never what the verb reaches.

Had the verse meant "the evil which He created," Arabic would build it the other way, with evil itself as the created object and a different pronoun tying it to the verb:

مِنَ الشَّرِّ الَّذِي خَلَقَ
"from the evil which He created."

That sentence uses الَّذِي and places evil under the verb, and the revelation does not say it.

So the lexical grounds come to two things a careful ear can catch:

- The construct اضافة makes evil belong to creation, rather than be a creation.
- The word مَا, standing as the object of "created," sets the made thing on one side and its possible evil on the other.

Read closely, the Arabic will not carry the harsher sense. It hands us evil as something that leans on the created world and is born from it — and our refuge is sought from that, never from the hand that shaped the world.
notes.anchor: which is wrong both theologically and lexically
notes.quote: which is wrong both theologically and lexically
etymology: خَلَقَ (He created): from the root خ-ل-ق, whose oldest sense is to measure out and proportion a thing. To create, in this root, is to shape by a fixed measure — seen in خَلْق (creation), خَٰلِق (Creator), and خَلَٰق (an allotted portion or due share). Allah creates by determining each thing's proportion, so the created order carries measure, not chaos.

مِن (from, of): the small particle marking source or origin, from the root م-ن-ن, which also yields مَنّ, a freely bestowed favour, and مَمْنُون, one on whom such favour is conferred. In this verse its work is exactly to point at where the evil comes out of — the created thing — rather than naming what was made.

notes.body:
Evil is real the way a shadow is real. A shadow has no substance of its own — only the place where light has been blocked — yet we can still stumble in it and hurt ourselves. Evil is not a thing Allah made and set loose in the world; it is what happens when a creature turns away from the divine nature and leaves a gap where goodness should be. **Evil exists as an absence, not as a substance.**

This is why the passage can call it "unreal" and still take it with deadly seriousness. Unreal does not mean imaginary or harmless. It means evil has no root of its own, no independent source — it borrows all its force from the good it corrupts, the way rust borrows the iron it eats. الحق, the Real, simply *is*; evil only happens, and only for a while, wherever creation deviates from its Maker.

So when the Quran tells us to seek refuge مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ
'from the evil of what He has created,'
Al-Falaq 113:2
we are not being warned about a rival power standing against Allah. **We are being taught to run from unreality back toward the Real.** Refuge is a direction we take, not a wall we raise against an equal.

Moral effort matters more because of this, not less. If good and evil were two equal forces, every struggle would hang in doubt. But because goodness is what truly is, each act of justice restores something real, and each evil is only a hole waiting to be filled. Fighting evil is the most natural thing in the world — like light returning to a dark room, where the darkness never had a chance.
notes.anchor: It is only a temporary state of deviation
notes.quote: It is only a temporary state of deviation
etymology: خلق (create): from the root خ-ل-ق, whose oldest sense is to measure something out and shape it to proportion. From it come خَلْق, the creation, and خالِق, the Creator who gives each thing its exact measure. To create is to set a thing in right proportion — so evil, a thing out of proportion, is a fracture in خلق itself.

حق (the Real, the truth): from the root ح-ق-ق, meaning to be firm, fixed, and established beyond doubt. The same root gives حقيقة, reality, and حق, a right or rightful due. What is utterly real and what is rightfully owed are one word — so evil, having no reality, can claim no حق and holds no ground of its own.

شر (evil): from the root ش-ر-ر, tied to شَرَر, flying sparks that scatter and consume. Evil carries that sense of scattering and breaking apart, the opposite of the gathering oneness of توحيد. It spreads like sparks yet, like sparks, holds no lasting substance once the fire it fed upon is gone.

notes.body:
When we look at the world with our two eyes, we see surfaces — shapes, colours, the outward face of things, what the tradition calls the ظاهر. The eye of the heart (عين القلب) is a different kind of seeing altogether. It looks not at the surface of a thing but at its inner reality, the باطن, and above all at whether a thing is truly grounded in Allah, who alone is fully real, الحق.

Here is why this eye sees evil as an illusion while our ordinary eyes feel it as solid and real. **Evil has no being of its own.** Think of darkness: it is not a substance Allah poured into a room, but simply the absence of light. A shadow looks like a thing, yet it owns no light and vanishes the moment the lamp is lit. Evil is like that shadow — real as an appearance, empty at its root, because it is only a turning-away from the goodness that is Allah's own nature.

Our physical eyes register the shadow and, quite naturally, take it for something. The eye of the heart sees further: it sees the light itself, and so it recognises the shadow for what it is — a lack, not a rival to the light. This is what it means to seek refuge in the Real from the unreal.

Now to the question everyone asks: is this a gift only for saints, or something we each carry? **Every one of us is born with the eye of the heart, but in most of us it sleeps under dust.** Consider three things that cloud it and one thing that clears it:

- Pride, which makes us gaze at ourselves instead of at Allah.
- Heedlessness, forgetting the source of all good.
- The appetites of the نفس, which make the shadow look beautiful.

What polishes the heart's eye is remembrance and prayer. In the prostration of سجدة we set the ego down, and a clean mirror begins to reflect. In Maulana Ali and in the Prophet this eye was fully open, which is why they could act with such certainty — they were seeing what most of us only believe.
notes.anchor: that eye which truly 'sees' God through
notes.quote: that eye which truly 'sees' God through
etymology: قلب (heart): from the root ق-ل-ب, meaning to turn over or to flip. The heart is named for its constant turning — shifting between states, moods, and convictions — which is exactly why it must be steadied and polished before its inner eye can see clearly.

بصيرة (insight): from the root ب-ص-ر, the same root as بصر, ordinary eyesight. Where بصر is the eye set in the face, بصيرة is the eye of the heart — inner sight, the discernment that grasps a reality the physical eye cannot reach.

حق (the Real): from the root ح-ق-ق, to be firm, fixed, and established as true. What is حق is what genuinely and unshakeably is; the word carries both 'truth' and 'rightful due', because what is real is what is owed.

باطن (the inner): from the root ب-ط-ن, meaning the belly or what lies hidden within. The باطن is the inward, concealed dimension of a thing, set against the ظاهر, its outward surface — the very layer the eye of the heart is made to perceive.

notes.body:
The answer lies less in that one sermon than in how the Imam *defines* justice. He does not describe it as one kindness set beside others. He gives it a definition that sets it apart from every other name:

وَضَعَ الشَّئُی حَقَّ مَحَلِّہِ
"Justice puts everything in its right place."

That definition changes everything. Mercy, wrath, and love each answer the question *what* — they are particular qualities that arrive in particular moments. Justice answers *where* and *how much*: it is the **ordering principle that hands every other quality its proper place and measure**. A quality standing among other qualities cannot be the root of them all; only the principle that arranges them can.

Consider mercy misplaced. Mercy poured out on a cruel oppressor while the wronged are left unhelped is no longer mercy — it has landed in the wrong place, and there it becomes an injustice. Mercy stays merciful only when it falls where it is due. So mercy leans on justice to remain itself, while **justice leans on nothing further** — placement itself can never be misplaced. That one-way dependence is why justice sits underneath the rest.

There is a deeper reason still, hidden inside a single word. Justice is bound to الحق, the Real, the absolutely true. To give each thing its حق is to honour what is genuinely real about it. Since Allah is الحق, His justice is His being the Real, ordering all that exists according to its truth — and His mercy, His wrath, His creating and His destroying are that same Real expressing itself rightly in each situation.

We can gather it into three points:

- Justice is defined as placement, not as a single feeling or response.
- Every other attribute must be rightly placed to be good, and that right placement is justice.
- Justice is one with الحق, so it orders reality rather than reacting inside it.

This is why the Imam can bear witness that Allah does not merely act justly but is Justice. The other names are the ways that one balancing truth reaches us; justice is the balance itself.
notes.anchor: it is the very essence of His nature
notes.quote: it is the very essence of His nature
etymology: عدل (justice): from the root ع-د-ل, whose core sense is to balance, to straighten, to make two sides equal. The same root yields اعتدال, equilibrium. So justice is not merely fairness but the holding of everything in even proportion, placing each thing exactly where its weight belongs.

محل (place): from ح-ل-ل, to alight, to settle, to come to rest. A محل is where something rightly comes to rest. The Imam's definition, putting each thing in its محل, pictures every being settling into the exact spot where it genuinely belongs.
